messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Stepwise rQTL-unknown warning messages and odd QTL curve
messages.body_plain:
I'm in the process of trying to run the multiple imputation method for this data set. With 1000 permutations to run, it is obviously a very slow process. Can I run the permutations in sets, and then use cbind() to combine the results together? If so, what do you suggest using as an appropriate permutation number and batch size? Using my old methods, for 1000 permutations, I was using a batch size of 100. Thank you.

On Wednesday, May 27, 2015 at 3:33:00 PM UTC-4, Karl Broman wrote:
> The warning message:
>
> Warning message:
> In lastout[[i]] - (max(lastout[[i]]) - dropresult[rn == qn[i], 3]) :
>   longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length
>
> is a bug that is revealed by the problem of having multiple QTL at very close to the same position, and this seems to arise because you have very strong QTL effects, and Haley-Knott regression isn't working well in this case.
>
> I'd recommend switching to the multiple imputation method (method="imp"): use sim.geno in place of calc.genoprob, and method="imp" in place of method="hk".
>
> karl

messages.body_plain:
Yes, I would run things in sets and combine them together afterwards.

The appropriate batch size depends on how many computers you have and how much memory they have available.

I would use all of the computers I have available, would pay attention to how much RAM is on the machine, and would only set as many simultaneous jobs running on a given computer so that they all fit into the available RAM.

I also generally aim for jobs that are ~4 hrs long, and then I'll set new jobs running when the old ones have completed. This way if something goes wrong, I'll know sooner rather than later.

karl

messages.subject_clean: Coding a factor as a covariate for QTL analysis
messages.body_plain:
For the data set I am working on, we decided we would like to include the grandmother and F1 mother as covariates. I am concerned that I have not coded these correctly into their numeric form, as when I added these two covariates, the computation time increased significantly.

There are four grandmothers and ten F1 females. This is approach I have taken:

>grandparent <- as.numeric(pull.pheno(sawfly.cross, pheno.col=20))

>fromg1 <- as.numeric(grandparent == 1)

>fromg2 <- as.numeric(grandparent == 2)

>fromg3 <- as.numeric(grandparent == 3)

>fromg4 <- as.numeric(grandparent == 4)

>grandparentx <- cbind(fromg1, fromg2, fromg3, fromg4)

I used similar coding to pull out the information for the F1 mothers. I then pulled all the covariates together using this code:

>allcovar <- cbind(head.covar, grandparentx, motherx)

Is this the right away to approach this? I will note that in the phenotype column, the grandparents or mothers are coded simply as 1-4 or 1-10.

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] best way to run scantwo permutations?
messages.body_plain:
We haven't implemented anything to assist with parallelizing across multiple nodes.
Functions that take n.cluster will use the multiple CPUs within a node, but not go across nodes.
Partly that's because different cluster setups tend to be so different.

Personally, I use a (now very old) perl script that generates a set of R scripts, one for each node, and then send those R scripts running separately.

karl

messages.body_plain:
1. If you type 'ls', R will print all of the code that defines the ls function. If you type 'ls()', R will execute that function. I think you left off the parentheses.

2. The default genotype codes for read.cross are "A", "H", "B"; if you've used different codes, you need to specify them via the 'genotypes' argument:

mycross <- read.cross("csv", file="myfile.csv", genotypes=c("AA", "AB", "BB"))

3. I'm guessing that you're referring to names like "c1.loc45", as in this example:

data(hyper)
hyper <-calc.genoprob(hyper, step=1)
out <- scanone(hyper)
summary(out, threshold=3)
##          chr  pos  lod
## c1.loc45   1 48.3 3.53
## D4Mit164   4 29.5 8.09

We assess association between genotype and phenotype at the markers and at a set of "pseudomarkers", whose positions are determined by the 'step' argument in calc.genoprob(). Names like c1.loc45 are these pseudomarkers.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Rather than do the calculations solely at the markers, we also consider positions between markers. This is in an attempt to get more precision information about the locations of QTL.

The summary output indicates the maximum LOD score on each chromosome and the position at which it was attained, which can be one of those pseudomarkers.

If you use step=0 in calc.genoprob, the calculations will be performed solely at the markers.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have been using the mqmfind.marker() function to pull out significant marker names and positional information from a MQM type R/qtl object.

In some cases there are >1 significant QTL per chromosome and the mqmfind.marker() function only returns one marker per chromosome.

I realize I could just extract all markers above my permutation threshold by subsetting a vector of LOD scores but this returns a lot of MQM pseudomarkers in addition to the actual markers within my genetic map.

Is there an alternative function or method that you folks prefer to use?

Max

messages.body_plain:
Alright, I've scripted out a quick and dirty work around. Here it is...

# Get a data frame of all significant markers (pseudomarkers included) with LOD score
sig.markers.pseudo <- out.mqm[out.mqm[,3] > mqm.permutation.threshold,]

# Use the function described below
sig.markers<-get_map_markers_from_mqm(sig.markers.pseudo)

# Here is the definition of the function

get_map_markers_from_mqm<-function(marker_list) {
  # Remove all pseudomarkers (c.#.loc#) to get just markers from map
  map_markers<-marker_list[grep('c[1:9]..*', as.character(marker_list[,1]), invert=T),]
  # Get a list of chromosomes to iterate through
  chrs<-sort(unique(map_markers$chr))
  # Construct a variable to store Markers found at peaks
  peaks<-c()
  # Iterate through list of chromosomes
  for(c in 1:length(chrs)) {
    # Get dataframe from individual chromosome
    temp<-map_markers[map_markers$chr == chrs[c],]
    # Is the first marker a peak?
    if (temp[1,4] > temp[2,4]) {peaks<-rbind(peaks, temp[1,])}
    # Is the last marker a peak?
    if (temp[nrow(temp),4] > temp[nrow(temp),4]) {peaks<-rbind(peaks, temp[nrow(temp),])}
    # Iterate through each marker and check if current marker's LOD score is greater than the LOD of two markers on either side
    for(r in 2:(nrow(temp)-1)) {
      # Check if value is actually a peak (get LOD left, middle and right)
      lod.l<-temp[r-1,4]
      lod.c<-temp[r,4]
      lod.r<-temp[r+1,4]
      # If marker in the center has higher LOD score than other two markers put into the 'peak' dataframe
      if ((lod.c > lod.l) && (lod.c > lod.r)) {peaks<-rbind(peaks, temp[r,])}
    }
  }
return(peaks) }

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] exporting to mapQTL format
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] exporting to mapQTL format
messages.body_plain:
write.cross with format="mapqtl" only works for phase-known 4-way cross data.

Your call to read.cross isn't really working properly. The genotypes vector for a 4-way cross needs to be a specific list of genotype codes, corresponding to these:
   1 = AC, 2 = BC, 3 = AD, 4 = BD,
   5 = A = AC or AD, 6 = B = BC or BD, 7 = C = AC or BC, 8 = D = AD or BD,
   9 = AC or BD, 10 = AD or BC,
   11 = not AC, 12 = not BC, 13 = not AD, 14 = not BD

So the data object in R is not really what you want, and while it thinks this is a 4-way cross, R/qtl can't convert it into the MapQTL format.

karl
